listening.title: University Open Day Visitor Route
listening.focus: Listening for times, locations and instructions
listening.script:
Maya: Good morning, welcome to Westfield University open day. How can I help you today?
Daniel: Hi, I have a booking for the general campus tour. I thought it started at 10 o'clock?
Maya: Good question. We actually moved the start time to 10:30 this morning because one of the guides was delayed. So please go to the Welcome Hall for 10:30.
Daniel: Okay, 10:30 at the Welcome Hall. Where exactly is that?
Maya: It's very easy to find. Come through the main entrance, walk straight past the reception, and it's right next to the library. There will be student helpers with blue shirts to show you the way.
Daniel: Great. How long is the tour and what will we see?
Maya: The tour lasts about an hour and a half. You'll visit the science laboratories, see an example of student accommodation, and finish at the sports centre where you can try the facilities.
Daniel: That sounds good. I'm also interested in the Business School. Is that part of the same route?
Maya: Not on the general route, no. But there is a separate Business School presentation at 1 p.m. in Room B12. For that one, you need to register first at the information desk in the Welcome Hall.
Daniel: I'll do that. Is there anywhere to get lunch on campus?
Maya: Yes, the Central Cafe on the ground floor of the Welcome Hall is open until 2 p.m. for visitors, and there's also an outdoor food market on the central square until 3 o'clock.
Daniel: Perfect. And finally, I drove here – is parking free for visitors today?
Maya: Yes, you can park for free in the North Car Park. Just take a ticket when you enter and then validate it – I mean, get it approved – at the Welcome Hall desk before you leave.
Daniel: Thanks so much, that's really helpful.
Maya: You're welcome. Enjoy your visit!

reading.title: City Household Recycling Feedback Scheme
reading.passage:
The city of Riverton introduced a household recycling-feedback scheme in early 2023 to address low recycling rates. Before the scheme, only 34% of household waste was correctly sorted, and collection teams reported high levels of contamination, such as food waste mixed with paper and unwashed containers. The council wanted a low-cost way to change behaviour without introducing fines, which had been unpopular in neighbouring areas. The council spent less than expected on printing and postage.

Under the new system, each participating household receives a monthly feedback card. The card shows three pieces of information: the total weight of correctly sorted recycling, the percentage of incorrect items, and a comparison with the average for their street. Households also receive short practical suggestions, for example rinsing containers before disposal and keeping paper dry. Participation is voluntary, and about 12,000 households joined in the first year. Cards are delivered together with the collection calendar, so residents do not need to use an app.

After six months, the council reported clear improvements. On average, correctly sorted recycling rose by 18% among participants, while contamination dropped from 22% to 14%. The improvement was not equal everywhere. In Elmwood, a neighbourhood with many young families, recycling increased by 27%, which the report presents as an example of strong engagement rather than proof that family households always recycle more. The council's main claim is that regular personalised feedback itself encourages better habits, not that any single neighbourhood represents the whole city.

The scheme also tested different types of feedback. One group received only numbers, a second group received numbers plus practical tips, and a third group received numbers, tips, and a comparison with neighbours. The third group improved the most, with a 24% increase, compared to 11% for the first group. This suggests that social comparison adds motivation beyond information alone. Surveys showed that many residents did not know that dirty packaging could spoil an entire batch of recycling, so the tips addressed a real gap in knowledge.

However, the scheme has limits. Households in rented accommodation improved less, possibly because they move more often and feel less connection to local programmes. The council now plans to develop a mobile app to provide weekly updates and to include renters more directly. Officials stress that feedback is a support tool, not a replacement for reliable collection services, and that long-term success will depend on both. Future funding will depend on whether these gains continue into the second year.
